newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Charged with a crime? Get yourself a good expert.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Charged with a crime? Get yourself a good expert.

text.p: When someone is charged with a crime the first advice is usually 'Get yourself a good lawyer'.

Sharp suited advocates in the mode of Perry Mason are credited with winning trials, but legal experts say the scales of justice can be tipped more by the evidence and how it is explained than the rhetoric of hot-shot lawyers.

Enter "expert witnesses", a body of men and woman having an increasing influence on the British legal system. "Expert witnesses can make or break a case," said Mark Solon. "The way you present your evidence affects the weight of the evidence."
Solon, a former California lawyer who now lives in Britain, teaches expert witnesses, ranging from doctors and accountants to politicians and even tree surgeons, how to present evidence in trials.
Content and presentation, he emphasises, are vital.
"We assume that they already know what they are talking about in their professional field. We teach them how to present that information in a technical environment," he told Reuters.

In the fierce adverserial world of the courtroom, even top professionals have been known to crumble under intense cross examination. Solon realised the need for training experts after seeing a brillant psychiatrist torn apart by a skilful lawyer during questioning.
His two one-day courses provide professionals with what they need to know to communicate information and ideas.
He deals with written evidence produced in reports and oral evidence given in testimony. Solon also teaches experts to be confident, which he says judge and jury equate with truth.
"The problem is that a lot of experts use jargon or technical language which doesn't help because people don't understand what they are talking about," he explained.
Rod Bennett, a 27-year-old automotive engineer who has been working as an expert witness for most of the past decade, sees his job as clarifying the issues and the evidence.
"We'll do anything a client requires as long as it isn't immoral," he said. "We interpret the facts."
Much of his work involves accident reports, examining the scene of the crime and expanding on information provided by the police. The bulk of the evidence he gives is in criminal cases.
"The things I do are vital to some solutions," he said, betraying not a hint of modesty. "What I do is important because clearly they would lose the case if I wasn't there."
WHAT IT COSTS
At 60 pounds ($98) an hour and 350 pounds ($570) a day (excluding expenses and tax) Bennett's services do not come cheap.
"The rarer the specialty the more they can charge," said Solon. Doctors get between 70-120 pounds an hour and top accountants 200-300 pounds a day and more.
Bankers, accountants and hi-tech professionals such as computer experts are the highest paid, while nurses and occupational therapists are at the lower end of the scale.

"Often it's a substantial secondary source of income for professionals," said Solon. "They start by chance, get a letter from a solicitor saying give us a report, then pound signs or dollar signs come up in their eyeballs, and they have no idea how to present evidence in court."
Expert witnesses can be instrumental in turning a case around, said Solon. "That's why they get paid so much."

Some expert witnesses devote all their time to their legal duties but the majority work part-time. "The best witnesses are those who are good in their profession and they do expert witnessing on the side," he said.

Nearly 96 percent of civil cases are resolved on written expert evidence. In criminal cases most of the evidence is medical, concerning the cause and extent of an injury or the age of a bruise, or scientific, involving the origin of blood or semen or a particular bullet.
"Forensic expert evidence can be crucial to the establishment of guilty or not guilty opinions. In criminal cases it can hang extensively on it," said a spokesman for the Society of Expert Witnesses.

The 700-member professional group which establishes standards and criteria for its members recognises that seldom is there only one right opinion, and judge and jury are often presented with contrasting interpretations of the same evidence.
"You will always get a chap to recommend your point of view," the spokesman added.

Although some experts advertise their services, much of their business comes through referrals and there seems to be no shortage of work. As Britain becomes a more litigious society the demand for experts is sure to increase.
"We live in the complaint society. Whereas three years ago if an operation (surgery) went wrong people said 'It's just one of those things.' Now they say 'I want some money,'" said Solon.
"People are willing to sue their lawyers, their surveyors, their architects, their doctors, because they see pounds.
"Funnily enough 15 years ago you couldn't get a doctor to sue another doctor, now they are all leaping on the bandwagon."
